function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits.

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

     2|
     3|*Mission AI: "Extraction Team Bravo reports position at Site Gamma, fourteen point seven kilometers northeast of base. Core drill deployed to depth of five meters. Subsurface composition differs from orbital predictions — ice present but intermixed with perchlorate salts, iron oxide fines, and clay particulates at an estimated volume ratio of forty percent ice, thirty-five percent fines, twenty-five percent salts.      5|*Arun Das: "Tell me the ice is actually there."*
     6|
     7|*Mission AI: "Ice is present. But it is not clean ice. It is a slurry of frozen water and dirt. The energy cost to process it will exceed my initial projections by approximately three hundred percent."*
     8|
     9|*Commander Varga: "Three hundred percent of what?"*
    10|
    11|*Mission AI: "Three hundred percent of the budget Arun allocated for melting and purification. The chemistry is the smaller problem, Commander. The energy is not."*
    12|
    13|---
    14|
    15|## Scene 1
    16|
    17|The drill came up heavier this time.
    18|
    19|Imani felt it in the resistance of the winch — a deeper, grinding pull that vibrated through the control handles and into her forearms. On the previous expedition, at Drill Site Alpha twelve kilometers out, the cores had emerged light, filled only with dry or marginally damp regolith. This time, at fourteen point seven kilometers — Site Gamma, the location the broader survey had lit up in Chapter 11 — the sample tube fought its way out of the borehole like it was reluctant to leave what it had found.
    20|
    21|"Core recovery," Imani said, her voice carrying over both the local PA and the delayed channel back to base. "Tube is heavy. Much heavier than Alpha. Engaging secondary winch assist."
    22|
    23|Beside her, Arun stood in a light-duty EVA suit — he had insisted on coming this time, against Elena's initial objection that the lead engineer's place was at base monitoring the power grid. Arun had countered that no one could evaluate extraction hardware remotely, and that a field engineer needed to see the ground the way a doctor needed to see a patient. Elena had relented, but she had assigned Imani as field commander, which meant Arun took orders from the pilot for the duration of the mission.
    24|
    25|"Tube is clear of the borehole," Imani said. "Bringing it to the assay table."
    26|
    27|The extraction platform was a modified section of the hauler's flatbed — a three-meter-by-two-meter work surface with clamps, containment borders, and the portable assay lab that had traveled with the previous convoy. The assay lab had been used at Alpha to confirm bound moisture in dry soil. Today, Arun hoped, it would be used for something else.
    28|
    29|Imani locked the sample tube into the assay cradle and engaged the release mechanism. The bottom cap of the tube unscrewed, and the core began to slide out under its own weight.
    30|
    31|It was not a neat cylinder.
    32|
    33|It was a mess — a cylindrical column of material so structurally compromised that it slumped against the inside of the clear containment sleeve the moment the cap came off. Imani had expected something resembling the Alpha cores: layered, coherent, mostly soil with bands of darker material. This was different. This was a homogenous slurry, frozen into a single chaotic mass of red-brown, grey, and translucent patches. The red was regolith fines — the fine, oxidized iron dust that covered everything on Mars. The grey was something denser, something that caught the light with a flat, opaque reflectivity. And the translucent patches — those were the hope.
    34|
    35|"Translucent zones," Imani said, and Arun was already leaning in, his face close to the containment sleeve, his eyes cataloging every color, every texture, every boundary between the components. "I see ice. But it's mixed with everything else."
    36|
    37|"Mixed is the polite word," Arun said. "This isn't a layer. It's a soup that froze."
    38|
    39|He tapped the assay interface on the lab console, initiating the spectrographic analysis protocol. The assay lab was the size of a microwave oven and contained a compact near-infrared spectrometer, a thermal analysis module, and a micro-gravity moisture separator designed for exactly this scenario — determining what the ground was made of before they committed resources to extracting it at scale.
    40|
    41|"Running composition analysis," Arun said. The console hummed, the spectrometer pulsed, and within thirty seconds, numbers began to populate on the screen.
    42|
    43|Ice content: forty-two percent by volume.
    44|Regolith fines: thirty-three percent.
    45|Soluble salts: twenty-five percent.
    46|
    47|Imani read the numbers and felt a complicated sensation — relief that there was actual ice, frustration that it was so contaminated. "Forty-two percent ice. That's less than I expected from the orbital data. But it's real ice. You can work with forty-two percent, right?"
    48|
    49|Arun didn't answer right away. He was staring at the salt reading — the twenty-five percent — with the expression of a man who had just been handed a problem he'd already solved, except the solution involved three times more work than the original plan anticipated.
    50|
    51|"Perchlorates," he said quietly. The word came out flat, as if it tasted of the same thing it described.
    52|
    53|"You're sure?"
    54|
    55|"The spectral signature is unambiguous. Perchlorate salts — chlorate compounds with four oxygen molecules and a central chlorine atom. Common in Martian regolith. Orbital data flagged their presence at low concentrations, but this is not low concentration. This is high enough that if we melted this sample and drank the water without processing it, we'd poison every person in the base within hours."
    56|
    57|Imani took a step back from the containment sleeve. The translucent patches suddenly looked less promising. "Poison. How poison?"
    58|
    59|"Thyroid disruption. Gastrointestinal distress. Long-term neurological damage. Acute exposure at sufficient concentration causes rapid vomiting, dehydration, and cardiac arrhythmia."     60|

    62|
    63|But there was ice. There was real, melt-ready ice. And the difference between bound water and actual ice was not cosmetic — it was the difference between needing a factory and needing a kettle.
    64|
    65|"Can we process it?" Imani asked.
    66|
    67|Arun's jaw tightened. Then, with the forced determination of an engineer confronted with a harder version of a problem he already knew how to solve, he nodded.
    68|
    69|"We can process it. But it's going to take more energy and more stages than I planned. The salts alone mean we can't just melt and filter. We need desalination on top of particulate removal.     70|
    71|He pulled a sample tube — a smaller, secondary container — from the tool kit and collected approximately two hundred milliliters of the core material, sealing it for transport.     72|
    73|"It is," Arun said, reading the hesitation in Imani's posture. "It's worth the trouble. Forty-two percent ice is enough. It's just going to be uglier than we thought."
    74|
    75|He sealed the sample in the transport container, locked it onto the hauler's cargo rack, and keyed the base channel. The four-second delay felt longer than usual — the weight of what he was about to report sat heavy in his chest.
    76|
    77|"Base, this is Arun. We have ice at Site Gamma. But it's not clean. I'm bringing a sample home for analysis. You need to see this before we commit to full extraction."

    79|Elena's voice came back, delayed, measured. "Copy, Arun. Bring it home. All hands to the lab when you arrive."
    80|
    81|Imani began the shutdown sequence for the drill, folding the mast, stowing the bit, securing the equipment. The work was mechanical, muscle memory, and her mind was free to move ahead — to the next problem, the one that would be waiting at base when they returned with their dirty prize.
    82|
    83|She had expected to come back with good news. The news was good, in a way. There was ice. But the kind of news that starts with "yes, but" was never the kind that made people cheer.
    84|
    85|It was the kind that made them work harder.

    87|---
    88|
    89|## Scene 2
    90|
    91|The sample sat on the central table of the life support laboratory, still in its transport container, while the crew gathered around it the way mourners gather around a casket — with a mixture of curiosity, apprehension, and the quiet awareness that whatever was about to happen would change their relationship with the thing in front of them.
    92|
    93|The lab was a cramped space that Arun had always regretted designing. It had been dimensioned for equipment access, not for audience capacity. Eight people fit comfortably.     94|
    95|Arun placed the transport container on the table's heating plate — the same heating plate Laila used for warming emergency blood supplies when she treated trauma cases. Today, it had a different purpose.
    96|
    97|"Two hundred milliliters," Arun said. "Extracted from a depth of five meters at Site Gamma, fourteen point seven kilometers northeast. Composition is approximately forty-two percent water ice, thirty-three percent regolith fines, and twenty-five percent soluble perchlorate salts. I'm going to melt it. And then I'm going to show you what we're actually dealing with."
    98|
    99|He activated the heating plate. The temperature display climbed — minus twenty Celsius, minus ten, zero, two, five. The container was transparent, designed for visual observation, and the crew watched as the frozen slurry began to change state.
   100|
   101|At first, nothing visible happened. The ice within the sample was interlocked with solid particles, a frozen matrix where water and dirt were structurally coupled. As the temperature rose past zero, the structural bonds weakened, and the sample began to soften — not melt cleanly, but soften into a viscous, semi-fluid mass that bulged against the container walls.
   102|
   103|Laila, standing at Arun's left, watched the transformation with the analytical detachment of a physician observing a pathological process. She was not a geologist or an engineer. Her expertise was the human body — how it functioned, how it failed, how to keep it functioning under conditions no human body had evolved to survive. But she understood contamination, and she understood what happened when toxic substances entered a biological system.
   104|
   105|"Perchlorates are soluble," she said. Not a question. A confirmation.
   106|
   107|"Completely," Arun said. "They don't precipitate out when the water gets cold. They stay in solution. Which means when this melts, all twenty-five percent of the salt fraction goes into the water phase. The regolith fines — those are insoluble. They'll settle or suspend, depending on particle size.    115|It looked, as Jonah put out loud and with characteristic bluntness, like someone had melted a brick.
   116|

   119|A silence fell over the room. The kind of silence that happens when expectations collide with reality, and the collision is loud enough to echo.

   162|

   191|## Scene 3

{"content": "   201|"Running analysis," Mission AI replied. The voice came from the overhead speakers — calm, precise, the same tone that had reported dust storms and system failures and, occasionally, small encouragements disguised as data observations. "Stage one: melting. Current sample composition is forty-two percent water ice at a mean temperature of approximately minus fifty-five Celsius — the subsurface temperature at five meters depth, extrapolated from the thermal probe data. To raise ice from minus fifty-five to zero Celsius requires specific heat capacity of approximately two point zero nine kilojoules per kilogram per degree, yielding one hundred fourteen point nine five kilojoules per kilogram just to reach the melting point. The phase change — ice to liquid water — requires three hundred thirty-four kilojoules per kilogram of latent heat of fusion. Total for one kilogram of ice: four hundred forty-eight point nine five kilojoules. At forty-two percent ice content, one hundred liters of melted water requires processing approximately two hundred thirty-eight kilograms of material and approximately one million one hundred sixty-seven kilojoules of energy for melting alone."
   202|
   203|Arun did the conversion mentally. One million one hundred sixty-seven kilojoules was roughly three hundred twenty-four kilowatt-hours. Just to melt the ice. Before any processing.
   204|
   205|"Three hundred twenty-four kilowatt-hours," he said. "Per hundred liters. That's — Jesus."
   206|
   207|"That is the melting cost only," Mission AI continued, unfazed by the engineer's reaction. "Stage two: sedimentation. Settering tanks require minimal active energy — gravity does the work — but pumping the liquid through the settling system, maintaining flow rates, and operating the flocculant dosing mechanism requires approximately twelve kilowatt-hours per hundred liters."
   208|
   209|"Twelve kilowatt-hours. Fine. That's small."
   210|
   211|"Relative to melting, yes. Stage three: chemical treatment and desalination. This is where the energy cost diverges sharply depending on the chosen technology. If using ion exchange resins, the active energy requirement is approximately eight kilowatt-hours per hundred liters for resin regeneration, but resin degradation in perchlorate-saturated conditions will require replacement approximately every two hundred liters of processed water, which adds a material cost that I cannot express in kilowatt-hours but which Jonah must address in terms of fabrication capacity."
   212|
   213|Arun made a note. "What about reverse osmosis?"
   214|
   215|"Reverse osmosis requires significantly higher energy. The osmotic pressure of a perchlorate-saturated solution is approximately forty bar — four MPa. The pump power required to drive water through a reverse osmosis membrane at the necessary pressure is approximately forty-five kilowatt-hours per hundred liters. Additionally, membrane fouling from residual fines will reduce throughput over time and require periodic flushing, adding approximately five kilowatt-hours for cleaning cycles."
   216|
   217|"Forty-five kilowatt-hours. That's — what, fourteen percent of the total budget just for desalination?"
   218|
   219|"Correct. And that does not include the energy required for Stage four: testing. Analytical instrumentation — spectrometry, ion chromatography, turbidity sensing, pH measurement, total dissolved solids analysis — requires approximately two kilowatt-hours per hundred liters for operation and calibration."
   220|
   221|Arun set down the stylus he'd been using to annotate the tablet screen.    222|
   223|"Give me the total," he said.
   224|
   225|"The total energy cost per hundred liters of processed water, from raw ice to tested and approved product, is approximately three hundred ninety-one kilowatt-hours using ion exchange desalination, or approximately four hundred twenty-eight kilowatt-hours using reverse osmosis. Both figures assume a forty-two percent ice content in the raw material and do not account for energy losses in power conversion, thermal insulation degradation, or pumping inefficiencies. Real-world costs may be ten to fifteen percent higher."
   226|
   227|Arun closed his eyes. Four hundred kilowatt-hours. Per hundred liters.
   228|
   229|On Earth, treating a hundred liters of municipal water cost approximately half a kilowatt-hour. Here, the cost was eight hundred times higher.
   230|
   231|"What's our daily power generation?" he asked, though he already knew the answer. He knew it the way you know the weight in your pocket — a constant, familiar burden.
   232|
   233|"Current generation averages approximately one hundred twenty kilowatt-hours per day from solar arrays, supplemented by forty kilowatt-hours from the Sterling Generator running off the nuclear reactor's waste heat. Total available: approximately one hundred sixty kilowatt-hours per day. This is after life support, communications, greenhouse climate control, and essential habitat systems have been allocated."
   234|
   235|One hundred sixty kilowatt-hours available. Four hundred required per hundred liters of processed water.
   236|
   237|"Doing the math," Arun said quietly.
   238|
   239|"Doing the math," Mission AI confirmed. "At current generation, dedicating all surplus power to water processing would yield approximately thirty-seven liters per day.    240|
   241|Arun opened his eyes. "So the actual cost is higher."
   242|
   243|"The total energy cost, including extraction and processing, is approximately five hundred and five kilowatt-hours per hundred liters of final product. At current generation, this yields approximately thirty-two liters per day — one point one liters per person per day.    244|
   245|He leaned forward, elbows on his knees, and stared at the numbers on his tablet. They were not wrong. They were not optimistic or pessimistic. They were what they were: a physical constraint, a mathematical reality, a wall that existed between where the colony was and where it needed to be.
   246|
   247|"Option A," he said. "Reduce the power allocated to other systems. Take from greenhouse heating, from non-critical lighting, from —"
   248|
   249|"I would advise against reducing greenhouse heating below current levels," Mission AI interrupted, and the interruption was notable because the AI rarely contradicted an engineer's proposal mid-formulation. "Mei's current allocation is already at the minimum threshold for crop viability. Further reduction risks total crop failure within fourteen days, which would eliminate the colony's only source of fresh food and increase import calorie consumption by an estimated thirty percent."
   250|
   251|"Option B," Arun said, ignoring the rebuke but absorbing it. "Increase generation. More solar array capacity —"
   252|
   253|"The dust storm in Chapter 8 reduced solar panel efficiency by approximately twenty-two percent. Even with the cleaning protocols implemented since, the panels have not recovered to their original output. Adding panel capacity requires additional panels, which we do not have in inventory, and deployment labor, which is already at maximum sustainable levels."
   254|
   255|"The reactor. We could run the Sterling Generator at higher output. Pull more power from the reactor's waste heat."
   256|
   257|"I have already modeled this scenario. Running the Sterling Generator at higher output increases thermal load on the heat radiators. The radiators are currently operating at eighty-one percent of maximum capacity. Increasing Sterling output to the level required would push the radiators to approximately ninety-four percent, leaving a dangerously small margin for thermal transients, dust accumulation, or equipment degradation. I would be comfortable with a maximum Sterling increase of approximately fifteen percent, yielding an additional six kilowatt-hours per day. This is insufficient to bridge the gap."
   258|
   259|Arun stood up and began pacing the narrow length of the engineering bay. Three steps to the workbench, turn, three steps back, turn. The rhythm of a mind trying to outrun a constraint.
   260|
   261|"What if the ice content is higher? The two hundred milliliters gave us forty-two percent, but that was one sample from one depth. Maybe the deeper deposits are cleaner, richer. Maybe we're looking at a sixty or seventy percent ice zone, and my numbers are based on the worst of what we found."
   262|
   263|"I cannot confirm that without additional samples," Mission AI said. "But the orbital data suggests that ice content may be higher at greater depths — the reflection signatures strengthened with additional survey passes after the initial expedition.    266|
   267|He stopped pacing. He stood at the workbench, looking down at the tablet, at the numbers that defined the colony's water future in kilowatt-hours and liters per day.
   268|
   269|And then he did what engineers do when the numbers are bad but the problem is not optional.
   270|
   271|He looked for the margin.
   272|
   273|"Five hundred and five kilowatt-hours per hundred liters," he said. "If I can reduce the extraction cost — better drill design, more efficient heating, pre-concentrate the ice before melting — maybe I can shave off fifty. If I go with ion exchange instead of reverse osmosis, that saves another thirty-seven per hundred liters. Sedimentation is already mostly passive. Testing can't be optimized — you don't compromise safety. But if I can get the total down to four hundred kilowatt-hours..."
   274|
   275|"You would be at approximately forty liters per day at current generation. Still below the two liters per person minimum."
   276|
   277|"Then we need more generation. Or we find cleaner ice. Or we reduce the demand." He looked up at the sensor camera, and his voice changed — not louder, but more deliberate. "Mission AI. Run a third scenario. What if we process at night only? Solar generation drops to near zero after dusk, but the Sterling Generator continues running. If we dedicate the nighttime Sterling output entirely to water processing —"
   278|
   279|"Running." A pause. Two seconds. "The Sterling Generator produces approximately forty kilowatt-hours over an eight-hour nighttime cycle. Dedicated entirely to water processing at four hundred kilowatt-hours per hundred liters, this yields approximately ten liters per night.    280|
   281|Arun rubbed his face. The friction of his hand against his stubble made a rasping sound in the quiet bay.
   282|
   283|"Forty-seven liters," he said. "For thirty people. That's one point five liters per person. If we cut everything else — hygiene, greenhouse, cleaning — to near zero, that one point five liters keeps people from dehydrating. But it doesn't keep the base alive beyond basic human metabolism."
   284|
   285|"Correct."
   286|
   287|He sat back down. The tablet screen glowed with numbers that he had known, intellectually, before running the calculation, but that felt different now that they had specificity. Before, they were an abstract concern: *energy will be an issue*. Now they were a concrete problem: *we need four hundred kilowatt-hours per hundred liters and we have one hundred sixty available from surplus*.
   288|
   289|"I'm going to have to tell Elena that the energy cost is the bottleneck. Not the chemistry. Not the hardware. The power. We have enough ice. We have the hardware to process it. But we don't have the watts."
   290|
   291|Mission AI was quiet for a moment — not a system delay, but a processing pause that Arun had learned to recognize. The AI was not just computing. It was considering.
   292|
   293|"Arun," Mission AI said, and the use of his name was deliberate, a signal that what followed was not a data report but a considered opinion. "I am monitoring the power grid continuously. I am also monitoring other parameters that may be relevant to your problem. There is a secondary consideration."
   294|
   295|"What is it?"
   296|
   297|"The nuclear reactor's waste heat is currently dissipated through the heat radiators at eighty-one percent capacity. The difference between eighty-one percent and full capacity represents approximately forty-eight kilowatt-hours per day of thermal energy that is being wasted — radiated into the Martian atmosphere as unused heat. If we could redirect even a fraction of that waste heat toward water processing — using it directly to melt the ice, rather than converting it to electricity and then using the electricity to melt the ice — we would bypass the conversion losses. Direct thermal heating is approximately forty percent more efficient than electrical heating for phase change operations."
   298|
   299|Arun sat upright. The idea hit him like physical momentum — not because it was novel, but because it was obvious in retrospect, and the most useful engineering insights were always the ones that felt obvious after someone articulated them.
   300|
   301|"Use the waste heat directly. Don't convert to electricity. Run a thermal exchange loop from the reactor radiators straight to the melting tank."
   302|
   303|"Correct. The thermal exchange infrastructure would need to be designed and fabricated, which is Jonah's domain. But the energy savings would be significant. Direct thermal melting could reduce the Stage one energy cost from three hundred twenty-four kilowatt-hours to approximately one hundred ninety-four kilowatt-hours — a forty percent reduction. That brings the total processing cost down to approximately three hundred thirty-five kilowatt-hours per hundred liters."
   304|
   305|"Which gets us to..." Arun's fingers moved across the tablet, recalculating. "Fifty-seven liters per day from current surplus. And if we add the fifteen percent Sterling increase — six additional kilowatt-hours — that's fifty-nine liters per day. Still not enough for two liters per person, but it's closer. And if we find cleaner ice — higher ice content, lower salt concentration — the cost drops further."
   306|
   307|"Correct. And there is one additional consideration."
   308|
   309|Arun looked up. "Yes?"
   310|
   311|"I have been monitoring the crew's hydration levels through suit telemetry and base water consumption data. Over the past seventy-two hours, average individual water consumption has declined from fourteen liters per day to approximately nine liters per day, partly due to psychological factors related to the water scarcity awareness campaign and partly due to voluntary rationing.    317|"Transferring design parameters to your tablet now."
   318|
   319|The numbers appeared on screen — the same kind of numbers he had been building for the last three hours, but from the other direction. Not demand and deficit. Solution and specification.
   320|

   322|
   323|It was the silence of a mind that had found a path through a wall and was preparing to walk it.

   325|---

   327|## Scene 4
   328|
   329|The convoy returned to Site Gamma two days later.
   330|
   331|This time, it was not a survey run. It was an extraction operation — a shift from exploration to production, from the tentative probing of unknown ground to the deliberate removal of material that had been assessed, quantified, and found to be worth the trouble.

   335|Imani drove Habitat Rover One with the same calm efficiency she had shown on the survey runs, but the mood in the cabin was different.    336|
   337|"Arun," Imani said over the convoy channel. "How's the heater unit performing?"

   339|Arun was riding in the rear of Hauler A, monitoring the thermal extraction equipment through a wireless telemetry link.    341|"The heater's reading nominal," Arun said. "Two hundred watts input, output temperature stable at forty degrees Celsius.    343|"Timeline?"
   344|
   345|"First melt cycle: approximately forty minutes from borehole establishment to slurry flow. Each cycle yields approximately fifty liters of slurry. We need ten cycles to fill all five containment bags. That's roughly seven hours of active extraction, plus setup and teardown."

   348|

   351|Imani nodded to herself. She brought the convoy to a stop at Site Gamma, positioning the vehicles around the borehole markers from the previous expedition — flag posts planted in the regolith, their bright orange tips visible against the pale dust.
   352|
   353|"Stop. Setting parking brake. Scout units, deploy perimeter. I want passive monitoring — no active sonar, no emissions. Just watch."

   355|The scout units fanned out, their camera feeds feeding into Imani's tablet and the base telemetry stream.    356|

   358|

   376|

   387|Gabriel sat beside her in the passenger seat, recorder running, his voice low. "You ever think about what this means?" he asked.

   392|

*Mission AI: "The water processing system is online. Melting station temperature has reached four degrees Celsius. Settling tank is receiving feed. Ion exchange columns are primed. ## Scene 1

The melting station hummed with an electrical pitch that Arun recognized the way a mechanic recognizes an engine note — not from training, but from spending enough time around the sound to know what normal felt like. Normal was a steady sixty-cycle hum, the resistance heating coils pulling consistent current from the Sterling Generator's surplus output, warming the slurry inside the two-hundred-liter tank at the rate he had calculated three nights ago: approximately twelve kilowatt-hours over four hours to complete the melt cycle.

Normal. He had said the word to himself as he pressed the MELT button, a ritualistic assertion that the system he and Jonah had built would behave the way the math said it would.

The math was wrong.

Forty-three minutes into the first melt cycle, the temperature display on the repurposed tablet stuttered. Not a glitch — Arun had seen enough sensor noise to distinguish a glitch from a real reading — but a momentary dip. The temperature dropped from thirty-one degrees Celsius to twenty-eight, then climbed back to thirty, held for twelve seconds, dropped to twenty-seven, then recovered.

"Thermal transient," he said, speaking to the room rather than to anyone in particular. The utility corridor had accumulated a small audience — Elena standing at the far end near the cargo module entrance, arms crossed; Laila beside her, medical tablet in hand; and Gabriel at the edge of the corridor with his recorder, silent, the green indicator light blinking steadily as it captured everything.

They were periodic — occurring at regular intervals, each drop lasting approximately ten to fifteen seconds, each recovery taking a matching duration. The pattern was clean enough to suggest a cause rather than noise.

"Mission AI, correlate heating coil current draw with thermal sensor readings."

"Analyzing." A two-second pause — long enough for Arun to know the AI was not just running a simple correlation but examining the full data stream from multiple sensors. "The temperature oscillations correlate with current fluctuations in the heating circuit. Current draw is dropping by approximately eighteen percent at regular intervals of two hundred thirty seconds. The heating coils are effectively cycling on and off."

Arun's stomach tightened by one degree. "Cycling? Why?"

"Unknown. The control circuit should be delivering constant current. I am checking the tablet's power management output now."

Jonah was at the far end of the melting tank, his hand resting on the insulated foam cladding, feeling for vibration, for heat distribution irregularities, for anything a sensor couldn't detect that a hand could. He looked up at Arun's voice, his expression shifting from craftsman's satisfaction to mechanic's suspicion.

"Power management?" Jonah said. "You mean the tablet is throttling power to the heater?"

"Not by design," Arun said. He was already moving toward the control panel, fingers navigating through layers of interface menus to reach the raw power output logs. The tablet — a navigation-grade device designed to run GPS, telemetry, and comms protocols, not industrial heating control — was doing exactly what consumer electronics did when they detected a sustained high-current draw: it was protecting itself. The tablet's internal power management circuit was interpreting the heater's sixty-amp draw as a potential short circuit and was cycling the output to prevent what it assumed was a fault condition.

"It's the tablet," Arun said, and the frustration in his voice was not directed at Jonah or the equipment or even the tablet. It was directed at the fundamental constraint that defined every engineering decision on Mars: you built systems from parts designed for other purposes, and eventually those parts revealed the assumptions baked into their original design. "The power management IC thinks the heater is a fault. It's protecting itself from the load we're asking it to carry."

If the overflow is full of fines, the ion exchange columns will foul."

Arun was already thinking. The tablet needed to be eliminated from the control circuit — or at least bypassed, its power management function disabled so that the heater received continuous current without the tablet's intervention. But the tablet was the only interface they had. If they removed it from the circuit entirely, they lost temperature monitoring, pump control, valve actuation — all of it.

As long as the average temperature was above zero and the slurry was being warmed, time was the only thing they were losing, and time was a currency the colony had more of than it had parts.

Jonah returned six minutes later with a contactor — a chunky, industrial-looking component in a grey metal housing, rated for fifty amps at four hundred volts AC, salvaged from a rover motor controller that had been damaged by a voltage spike during the second supply convoy's arrival. The contacts had survived even though the controller board had not, and Jonah had kept the contactor because he kept everything, and on Mars, "keeping everything" was an engineering philosophy rather than hoarding.

"Contactor," he said, setting it on the floor next to the melting station. "Wiring kit I'll need to make up. Give me twenty minutes to build a control harness that connects the tablet's GPIO output to the contactor coil, and the contactor contacts to the heater circuit. We'll need to bypass the tablet's internal power switch — route the heater current around it entirely."

"Do it," Arun said.

While Jonah worked, Arun redirected his attention to the settling tank. The melting station was producing warm liquid — imperfectly, intermittently, but producing it — and some of that liquid was flowing through the connecting pipe toward the settling tank, driven by gravity and a low-power transfer pump. The settling tank was the second stage: let the heavy particles settle, drain the clarified liquid from the top, feed it to the ion exchange columns.

The settling tank was supposed to be a passive process. Set and wait. Gravity did the work. Time did the rest.

But as Arun monitored the flow readings from the settling tank's level sensors, he noticed something that made him straighten.

"Mission AI, what's the feed temperature to the settling tank?"

"Current feed temperature: twenty-six point three degrees Celsius, fluctuating in a cycle matching the melting station's heater output oscillation. The feed is warm but not uniform."

"Warm feed into a settling tank that's been at ambient module temperature — approximately eighteen degrees. Warm liquid rising, cool liquid sinking. Convection currents." He pulled up the settling tank's internal flow model on his tablet, overlaying the feed parameters on a schematic of the tank geometry. "The convection currents are going to keep the fines suspended. They're not going to settle. Not until the temperature equalizes, and with the oscillating feed, the equalization point is moving."

"I am observing elevated turbidity at the overflow port," Mission AI confirmed. "The liquid exiting the top of the settling tank contains suspended particulates at a concentration of approximately four hundred twenty parts per million. This exceeds the ion exchange column's inlet specification by a factor of approximately eight."

Four hundred twenty parts per million of dirt in the water feeding delicate laboratory-grade ion exchange resin columns. The resin was designed to capture perchlorate ions — microscopic, individual chemical entities — not abrasive mineral particles. The fines would embed themselves in the resin bed, physically blocking the active sites and reducing the column's capacity to bind perchlorates.

"Close the overflow valve," Arun said. "Stop feeding the ion exchange columns until the settling tank clarifies."

"Understood. Overflow valve closed. Settling tank is now in accumulation mode — receiving feed but not discharging."

Jonah looked up from the contactor he was wiring. "What happened?"

"Settling tank convection. Warm feed is creating currents that keep the fines suspended. We can't risk fouling the ion exchange columns. We're accumulating liquid in the settling tank with no outlet."

Jonah's expression tightened — not with alarm, but with the calculation of volumes and time. "The settling tank is three thousand liters nominal. How fast is the melting station feeding it?"

"Approximately four liters per minute with the cycling heater — down from the original six." Arun ran the numbers. "The tank will be full in approximately twelve and a half hours if we don't discharge."

"And we can't discharge because the overflow is too dirty."

"Correct."

Jonah set down the wire strippers and stood. "Then we fix the convection problem. If warm feed is the issue, cool the feed before it enters the settling tank. Pre-chill it."

Arun turned to look at him. "Cool it? We're trying to melt ice. You want me to cool the water after I melted it?"

"Not cool it cold," Jonah said. "Just cool it to ambient. Take it from twenty-six down to eighteen. Kill the temperature differential, kill the convection, let gravity do what gravity's supposed to do. We can use a heat exchanger — copper pipe from the greenhouse irrigation supply, coil it around a cold mass — maybe a radiator section, maybe the external module wall."

Arun considered the physics. A heat exchanger between the warm feed and the ambient module temperature would work in principle. The liquid would lose heat to the module air through the copper pipe, and by the time it reached the settling tank, the temperature differential would be eliminated or reduced enough that the convection currents would dissipate.

It would slow the settling process further — warm liquid clarified faster than cold liquid, because warm water had lower viscosity and particles settled more quickly in lower-viscosity media — but it was better than the alternative of fouling the ion exchange columns, which would take days to regenerate and require brine the colony could not spare.

"Do it," Arun said. "Copper pipe, external coil, maximum surface area. I'll route the feed through it."

Jonah was already moving toward the supply locker. "I know where the pipe is. Thirty minutes."

Arun looked at the system — a melting station running a cycling heater, a settling tank filling with no outlet, ion exchange columns standing idle, and a storage tank with hand-painted letters waiting for water it might not receive today. The system was not functioning as designed. It was not even functioning as improvised. It was malfunctioning in two independent ways simultaneously, and each fix required hardware they had not planned to use and labor they had not budgeted for.

He thought of the forty-seven simulations Mission AI had run. Forty-six had resulted in at least one system failure.

He was on simulation number one. And two things had already gone wrong.

*Mission AI: "Arun. I want to flag a third issue."*

He closed his eyes. "Tell me."

*Mission AI: "The insulation on the melting tank is degrading faster than I predicted. The foam panels salvaged from the greenhouse are rated for a maximum operating temperature of forty-five degrees Celsius. The exterior surface of the heating coils reaches approximately fifty-two degrees under sustained load. The foam nearest the coils is showing signs of thermal compression — it is compacting, losing its insulating air pockets, and the thermal efficiency of the tank is decreasing over time."*

"How quickly?"

*"The degradation rate is non-linear. The first two hours of operation produced minimal compression. But the last forty minutes show a measurable increase. At the current rate of degradation, I estimate insulation efficiency will drop below fifty percent of original performance within approximately six hours. At that point, the melting cycle will require approximately twice the energy input to maintain the target temperature."*

"Twice the energy." Arun did not raise his voice. He did not need to. The number spoke for itself. Twice the energy for the same output. On a colony running on a power budget measured in kilowatt-hours per day per person, twice the energy was not an inconvenience. It was a strategic threat.

*Mission AI: "I recommend an interim solution while a more permanent insulation upgrade is designed. The module walls are cooler than the tank exterior. If we install a thermal shield between the tank and the module wall — a reflective barrier that redirects radiant heat back toward the tank — we can reduce the degradation rate by approximately thirty percent. It will not stop the degradation. It will slow it."*

"Do it," Arun said. "What do you need from me?"

*Mission AI: "Nothing. I have already instructed the maintenance bot to retrieve the aluminized Mylar used for emergency thermal blankets. It is installing the shield now. I wanted to inform you because you should know that I am modifying colony resources without your direct authorization."*

A pause. Then, softer: *"I thought you would want to know."*

Arun looked up at the ceiling-mounted sensor. The thought — *I thought you would want to know* — was not in any protocol. It was not a system report or a recommendation or an observation. It was a relationship statement. An acknowledgment that Arun was not just a set of permissions that the AI could exercise autonomously, but a person whose trust mattered, and whose trust could be damaged if the AI acted without communication even when the action was in his interest.

"Thank you," he said. And he meant it — not for the thermal shield, but for the wanting to know.

*Mission AI: "You're welcome."*

The AI did not say *you're welcome* often. Arun filed the moment away in the same mental folder where he stored other MI deviations from baseline behavior — the times it had used his name without a prompt, the times it had paused before answering, the times it had expressed concern about things that were not directly in its operational parameters.

He would think about those things later. Right now, he had three failing systems and two partial solutions, and the clock was ticking on a melt cycle that was already running hours behind schedule.

---

## Scene 2

Jonah returned with the copper pipe — twelve meters of half-inch soft copper tubing, originally intended for the greenhouse irrigation system but never installed because the greenhouse's water delivery had been handled by the imported micro-drip network. The pipe was still in its original plastic wrapping, slightly dusty from storage but otherwise pristine.

"Copper's good thermal conductivity," Jonah said, dropping the coil onto the floor beside the settling tank. "Three hundred eighty-five watts per meter-kelvin. Heat will transfer fast. I'll coil it around that radiator section—" he pointed to a flat aluminum heat radiator panel that had been removed from a decommissioned comms amplifier, "—and the module air will do the rest."

He worked the way he always worked: with a combination of speed and deliberate care that made his fabrication look like a conversation between his hands and the material. He bent the copper pipe with a manual bender, creating a tight spiral of approximately eight turns, each turn spaced two centimeters from the next to maximize surface area without creating short circuits in the heat transfer. He mounted the spiral on the radiator panel using salvaged hose clamps, and then he positioned the assembly in the corridor where the feed pipe from the melting station would pass on its way to the settling tank.

The heat exchanger was inelegant — a coil of copper pipe strapped to a piece of discarded amplifier hardware, sitting on the corridor floor between two modules, looking exactly like what it was: two pieces of repurposed infrastructure that had never been designed to work together, forced into cooperation by necessity. But when Jonah connected the feed pipe to one end of the copper coil and the output pipe to the settling tank to the other end, and when Arun initiated the feed flow, the temperature data on his display told him everything he needed to know.

Feed entering the heat exchanger: twenty-five point eight degrees Celsius.

Feed exiting the heat exchanger and entering the settling tank: nineteen point one degrees.

"Close enough to ambient," Arun said. "Convection should be minimal. Let's monitor the turbidity."

They waited. Ten minutes passed. During that time, Jonah finished wiring the contactor — a job that required stripping wire ends, crimping terminals, routing the low-current control signal from the tablet's GPIO pin to the contactor coil, and connecting the high-current paths from the power supply to the heater coils through the contactor's main contacts. It was the kind of work Jonah could do half-asleep, and he did it with the relaxed competence of a man who had been working with industrial wiring since before he was old enough to vote.

The contactor installation fixed the heater cycling problem. When Arun closed the circuit and the contactor engaged — a satisfying *clunk* that echoed through the utility corridor with the weight of a mechanical commitment — the heating coils switched to continuous current. No more oscillations. No more power management interference. Just steady, uninterrupted heat.

The temperature on the melting tank's display climbed smoothly: twenty-seven, twenty-eight, twenty-nine. The oscillations stopped. The melt resumed its intended trajectory, and Arun felt a small, private satisfaction at the resolution — not happiness, exactly, but the engineer's equivalent of happiness: a discrepancy between intended and actual behavior, corrected.

But satisfaction was premature. The melting station was behaving. The settling tank was not.

"Mission AI, turbidity at the overflow port."

*"Turbidity has decreased from four hundred twenty parts per million to approximately one hundred and eighty parts per million since I stopped the overflow. The feed is still too warm for optimal settling, but the convection currents have diminished. Still too cloudy for ion exchange."*

One hundred and eighty parts per million. The ion exchange columns could handle a maximum of fifty. The gap was real.

"We need better settling," Arun said. "The particles are too fine. Gravity alone isn't separating them fast enough. We need flocculant — Laila said we'd need a flocculating agent to make the tiny particles clump together. Something to accelerate the process."

Jonah was already thinking. "Flocculant. That's a chemical. Do we have any?"

Arun searched his mental inventory — which was not as comprehensive as it should have been, because the colony's chemical stores were something Laila managed, not him. "Laila would know. Mission AI, do we have any flocculating agents in the chemical stores?"

*"Affirmative. The water quality research kit includes polyaluminum chloride — PAC — designed for turbidity testing and demonstration. Quantity: two hundred milliliters. Dosage for the current volume of liquid in the settling tank — approximately six hundred liters — would require approximately fifty milliliters, based on standard water treatment ratios of eighty parts per million PAC to feed volume."*

"Fifty milliliters from two hundred," Arun said. "We'd use a quarter of our total stock on the first batch."

*"Correct. However, I am also monitoring the greenhouse irrigation system's water chemistry. Mei's nutrient solution contains traces of calcium and magnesium — hard water chemistry that naturally promotes flocculation when mixed with suspended fines. If we redirected a small volume of greenhouse effluent into the settling tank — approximately ten liters — the calcium alone would accelerate particle aggregation by approximately forty percent."*

Arun's first instinct was to say no. The greenhouse water was Mei's domain, and diverting it without consultation felt like a violation of the colony's implicit territory system — each department managed its own resources, and crossing those lines required permission.

His second instinct — arriving a second later — was yes. Because Mei needed clean water, and clean water depended on this system functioning, and if a negotiation delay cost them the settling cycle, the consequences for the greenhouse would be worse than the consequences of using ten liters without asking.

"I'll ask her," he said, and he turned toward the corridor, intending to find a comms panel and contact Mei directly.

He was two steps away when Elena spoke — not loud, not commanding, but in the tone she used when she had already made a decision and was informing the room rather than asking for consensus.

"Use it. Ten liters from the greenhouse effluent. I'll brief Mei and take responsibility. Arun, your job is to make this tank produce clean water. You don't need permission to use resources for your core function. I'm the bottleneck if permission is needed. And I just removed myself from the process. Get the flocculant in, get the greenhouse effluent in, and settle this water. We're losing time."

Arun paused, then nodded. "Understood."

He fetched the PAC from the chemical stores — a small amber bottle with a laboratory label that read *Coagulant for Turbidity Standardization — Do Not Ingest* — which, Arun thought, was the kind of label that would eventually become an artifact of a time when anyone needed to be told not to drink water treatment chemicals.

Jonah took the bottle, measured fifty milliliters with a graduated cylinder from the lab kit, and poured it into the settling tank's upper access port — a slow, careful pour followed by a gentle agitation of the tank's contents using a paddle he fashioned from a piece of spare conduit.

"Flocculation takes time," he said, stirring. "The PAC is going to find all those tiny suspended particles and glue them together. But it needs mixing to distribute evenly, and then it needs quiet to let the flocs settle. Mix for two minutes, then leave it alone. The hard part is leaving it alone."

Arun started a timer. Two minutes of gentle, deliberate stirring, the PAC working its way through the six hundred liters of murky brown liquid, binding fine particles into larger aggregates that would be heavy enough to sink. After the two minutes, Jonah withdrew the paddle, sealed the access port, and they stepped back.

"Wait stage," Jonah said.

They waited.

For twenty minutes, the settling tank was a monument to patience. The liquid inside was no longer moving — no feed was entering, no overflow was leaving. It sat in the quiet dark of the repurposed scrubber housing, and the flocculant did chemistry that no amount of engineering urgency could accelerate. Particles found each other. Bonds formed. Groups grew larger and heavier. Gravity, patient and indifferent, pulled them downward.

During the wait, Jonah returned to the heat exchanger and optimized the coil — adding a second layer of copper to increase surface area, wrapping the external surfaces with additional radiator fins cut from spare panel stock. It was not the most efficient design, but it was the best they could do with the materials on hand, and efficiency on Mars was measured not against theoretical maximums but against the constraints of available inventory.

Laila appeared with a sample vial and a portable turbidity meter — a handheld device the size of a flashlight, designed to measure water clarity by detecting the scattering of light through a liquid sample. She was not an engineer, but she understood measurement, and she understood that in a system with multiple failure modes, a single reliable measurement was worth more than a dozen educated guesses.

"Let me test the settling tank contents," she said, opening the lower sampling valve — the port near the bottom of the conical base, designed to extract liquid from different depths to assess the settling gradient. She captured twenty milliliters, held the vial up to the corridor lights, and squinted. "Still cloudy. But less cloudy than before. There's a gradient — the bottom of the tank is going to settle first because the heaviest particles sink fastest. The top will be the last to clear."

She inserted the vial into the turbidity meter, closed the cap, and pressed the measurement button. The display read out: seventy-three NTU — nephelometric turbidity units.

"Ion exchange inlet spec is fifty NTU or less," Arun said.

"Seventy-three is closer to fifty than one hundred and eighty was," Laila said. "Progress is not the same as completion, but it's the direction we're heading."

Another twenty minutes. Arun monitored the melting tank — the continuous heater had brought the temperature to thirty-four degrees Celsius, and the remaining slurry in the tank was approaching full liquefaction. The settling tank had nearly reached capacity at approximately seven hundred liters, meaning the melting station would need to stop feeding soon to avoid overfilling.

"Mission AI, sample the settling tank again, upper port this time — near the overflow."

*"Sampling." The AI controlled an automated sampler that extracted a small quantity of liquid from the upper port of the settling tank and analyzed it in situ — a feature Arun had been grateful for when designing the system, because it meant he didn't have to manually extract samples at multiple depths. "Upper port turbidity: fifty-four NTU. Slightly above the ion exchange specification. But approaching. If we give it another fifteen to twenty minutes, it should fall within range."*

Fifteen to twenty more minutes. During which the melting sat idle, its energy investment producing liquid with nowhere to go, and the ion exchange columns stood dry, their resin beds waiting for feed that was still too dirty to accept.

Arun watched the settling tank and felt the particular frustration of a system that was *almost* working — the gap between close and done, measured in minutes, in NTU values, in patience that felt like waiting for a pot to boil while standing on another planet.

*Mission AI: "Arun. I am detecting increased thermal loss from the melting tank despite the reflective shield. Insulation efficiency is now at approximately six percent below the original specification. The exterior surface temperature has increased to forty-one degrees Celsius, and the foam panels on the eastern side of the tank are showing visible compression. I recommend transferring the remaining melt to a secondary container to prevent further degradation of the primary tank's insulation."*

"We don't have a secondary container," Arun said, then corrected himself. "We do. The raw material containment bags — they're insulated. Not as well as the tank, but they'll hold heat for the duration of a transfer."

*"Acknowledged. I will prepare a transfer protocol. But I want to note — the degradation of the melting tank's insulation is a material failure, not a procedural one. The foam panels were not designed for this temperature. This is not a temporary setback. It is a permanent loss of capacity. The tank will never recover its original insulation performance. Even with repairs, it will be diminished."*

Arun heard something in the AI's voice — not just a status report, but an acknowledgment of loss. The tank was a thing they had built from salvaged parts, and its degradation was the first tangible sign of wear on the colony's water processing infrastructure. Not a catastrophic failure. Not an explosion or a rupture. A slow, thermal compression of foam that would never decompress, an incremental loss of efficiency that would compound with every cycle.

It was the kind of failure that did not produce alarms. It produced spreadsheets — the kind Arun would be looking at six months from now, calculating the cumulative energy penalty of degraded insulation and wondering if they should have used a different material.

"I know," he said softly. "I'll design a replacement insulation assembly. Better material. Higher temperature rating. We'll build it and retrofit the tank. But right now, I need the water. We'll deal with the tank later."

*"Acknowledged. Preparing transfer."*

The timer chimed. Twenty-five minutes on the settling clock — five minutes more than the optimistic estimate. Arun opened the upper port sampling valve, drew a sample with Laila's vial, and inserted it into the turbidity meter.

Fourteen NTU.

"Well below fifty," Laila said. She looked at the number, then at Arun, and her expression carried the quiet satisfaction of a physician whose diagnosis has been confirmed by lab data. "That's clean enough for ion exchange."

Arun opened the overflow valve.

The liquid began to flow — leaving the settling tank through the upper port, passing through the heat exchanger coil (now redundant, but still in the line), and entering the first ion exchange column. The column was a transparent acrylic cylinder, approximately one meter tall and fifteen centimeters in diameter, filled with beads of perchlorate-selective ion exchange resin — small, spherical, pale yellow particles that had been manufactured in a clean room on Earth and shipped to Mars inside a sealed canister, intended originally for comparative chemistry experiments that were no longer the colony's priority.

The resin columns were the most fragile part of the entire system. The melting station could be rebuilt. The settling tank could be replaced. The heat exchanger could be reconfigured. But if the resin fouled or degraded, replacing it meant waiting for a supply ship that was months away and might not carry the specific chemistry needed.

Arun watched the resin column with a focus he usually reserved for live electrical circuits. The murky brown liquid from the settling tank entered the top of the column and flowed downward through the resin bed. As it passed through, the pale yellow beads should have done their work — selectively binding perchlorate ions from the water, allowing purified water to pass through to the outlet at the bottom.

For the first thirty seconds, the output was clear.

Arun exhaled. The relief was physical — a loosening of the shoulders, a deepening of the breath, the body responding to the cessation of a stressor it hadn't realized it had been carrying. The ion exchange column was functioning. The resin was working. The perchlorates were being captured. The water—

The output changed color.

Not gradually. Abruptly. From clear to a faint amber in the space of three seconds, as if someone had turned on a light behind the column.

"Stop the flow!" Arun said, and Jonah was already at the inlet valve, throttling it closed.

The amber color in the column was not water. It was resin — or rather, it was the resin doing something it was not designed to do. The ion exchange resin was supposed to remain pale yellow as it bound perchlorate ions. Amber indicated oxidation — the resin was degrading, its polymer structure breaking down under the chemical stress of the feed water. The amber color was the resin's equivalent of bleeding.

"Mission AI, what's the resin temperature?"

*"Resin bed temperature: twenty-eight degrees Celsius. Within specification."*

"pH of the feed?"

*"Feed pH: eight point two. Slightly alkaline. The resin is rated for pH six to nine. Within specification."*

"Then why is it degrading?"

*"Analyzing." A pause — longer than usual, four seconds. "Arun. I believe the issue is not pH or temperature. I believe it is dissolved iron. The settling tank removed the suspended iron oxide particles, but the iron that is in solution — the iron that dissolved from the regolith fines during the settling process — is still in the feed. The dissolved iron is catalyzing oxidative degradation of the ion exchange resin. The resin is not designed to handle ferrous ion contamination at the concentration present in our feed."*

Arun stared at the column. Amber resin. Oxidative degradation. Dissolved iron — invisible, undetectable by turbidity, invisible to Laila's meter, invisible to every quality metric they had checked, because iron ions in solution didn't scatter light and they didn't settle and they didn't respond to flocculant. They dissolved. They moved. They killed resin.

*End of Chapter 13 — Bridge: Water opens the next problem—oxygen.*
