## Scene 1

The melting station hummed steady, the resistance heating coils pulling consistent current from the Sterling Generator's surplus output, warming slurry inside the two-hundred-liter tank at the rate Arun had calculated three nights ago: approximately twelve kilowatt-hours over four hours.

Normal. He had pressed the MELT button and said the word to himself — a ritual assertion that the system he and Jonah had built would behave the way the math said it would.

Forty-three minutes in, the temperature display stuttered.

Not a glitch. The drop from thirty-one degrees to twenty-eight was too clean, too repeatable — climbing back to thirty, holding twelve seconds, dropping to twenty-seven, recovering. Periodic. Rhythmic. Wrong.

"Thermal transient," Arun said. Elena stood at the corridor entrance, arms crossed. Laila beside her, medical tablet in hand. Gabriel hovered at the edge with his recorder, the green light blinking.

"Mission AI, correlate heating coil current draw with thermal sensor readings."

"Analyzing." Two seconds. "Temperature oscillations correlate with current fluctuations. Current is dropping by approximately eighteen percent at intervals of two hundred thirty seconds. The heating coils are cycling on and off."

Arun's stomach tightened. "Why?"

"Unknown. The control circuit should deliver constant current."

Jonah's hand was already on the tank's insulated cladding, feeling for heat distribution irregularities the way he felt for weld imperfections — by touch, by twenty years of working with metal. "Power management?" he called over. "The tablet is throttling?"

"Not by design." Arun navigated to raw power logs. The navigation-grade tablet was doing exactly what consumer electronics did under sustained high-current draw: protecting itself. It was interpreting the heater's load as a potential short and cycling output. "The power management IC thinks the heater is a fault."

"So the heater pulses," Jonah said. "Melt cycle takes —"

"Much longer. And the temperature inconsistency creates problems downstream. Unstable convection in the settling tank means particles don't settle. If particles don't settle, the clarified overflow carries fines. Fines reach the ion exchange columns, the resin fouls."

Elena uncrossed her arms. "Solution."

"Bypass the tablet from the heater circuit. Jonah — do we have a contactor? Something that switches the heater load directly from a low-current signal?"

"Contactor, yes. Spare from the rover motor controller — fifty-amp. I can build a control harness. Twenty minutes." He was already moving.

Laila stepped forward while Jonah worked. "How long does this add?"

"At least forty percent to the cycle. Maybe more. The oscillation means the coldest slurry chunks experience thermal cycling instead of continuous heating."

"Greenhouse needs water on a three-day cycle. Mei's plants are showing stress."

"We'll make up time running parallel cycles. But this first batch — slower than planned."

"Slower is not failed," Laila said. The physician's calibration: adjusting expectations to reality rather than hoping reality adjusted to the plan.

The temperature dipped again. Twenty-seven. Hold. Climb. Thirty.

Jonah returned with the contactor — chunky, industrial, grey metal housing, salvaged from a rover controller fried by a voltage spike. He kept it because he kept everything, and on Mars, keeping everything was philosophy, not hoarding.

Twenty minutes later he had it wired: tablet GPIO driving the contactor coil at half an amp — well below the protection threshold — the contactor's main contacts switching the full heater load. When Arun closed the circuit, the contactor engaged with a satisfying *clunk* that echoed through the corridor. Mechanical commitment.

The coils hit continuous current. Temperature climbed smoothly: twenty-seven, twenty-eight, twenty-nine. The oscillations stopped. The melt resumed.

Small satisfaction, the engineer's equivalent of happiness: a discrepancy between intended and actual, corrected.

Arun turned to the settling tank. The melting station was feeding it warm liquid through a connecting pipe, gravity and a low-power pump doing the work. The settling tank was supposed to be passive — set and wait, gravity did the work, time did the rest.

Something in the level readings caught his eye.

"Mission AI, feed temperature to the settling tank."

"Twenty-six point three degrees Celsius. Fluctuating with the heater oscillation." The AI corrected itself. "The oscillation has stopped. Feed temperature is now stable at twenty-six point three. But the settling tank is at ambient — eighteen degrees."

"Warm feed into a cool tank." Arun pulled up the flow model. "Convection currents. Warm liquid rising, cool sinking. The currents are keeping fines suspended."

"I am observing elevated turbidity at the overflow port — approximately four hundred twenty parts per million. This exceeds the ion exchange specification by a factor of eight."

Four hundred twenty parts per million in water destined for delicate laboratory-grade resin. The fines would embed in the resin bed, blocking active sites.

"Close the overflow valve," Arun said. "We accumulate until it clarifies."

"Overflow closed. Settling tank in accumulation mode."

Jonah read the situation from the data. "How long until full?"

"Twelve and a half hours if we don't discharge. At current feed rate."

"And we can't discharge because it's too dirty." Jonah considered for three seconds. "Cool the feed. Kill the temperature differential, kill the convection. Heat exchanger — copper pipe from greenhouse irrigation, coil it around a cold mass."

"After I melted it, you want me to cool it."

"Not cold. Ambient. Just take it down from twenty-six to eighteen. Copper's three hundred eighty-five watts per meter-kelvin. Heat transfers fast. I'll rig a coil around that radiator panel from the old comms amplifier."

Arun considered the physics. Warm feed through a copper coil exposed to module air — it would lose heat, the temperature differential would collapse, convection would stop. It would slow settling slightly — warm water clarified faster than cold, lower viscosity, particles settled quicker — but it was better than fouling the resin columns, which would take days to regenerate.

"Do it."

*Mission AI: "Arun. Third issue."*

He closed his eyes briefly. "Tell me."

*"The insulation on the melting tank is degrading. The foam panels from the greenhouse are rated for forty-five degrees. The heating coil surfaces reach fifty-two. Foam near the coils is showing thermal compression — losing insulating air pockets. Efficiency decreasing."*

"How fast?"

*"At current rate, insulation efficiency drops below fifty percent within approximately six hours. The melting cycle will require roughly twice the energy."*

Twice the energy. On a colony running on a budget counted in kilowatt-hours per person per day, twice the energy was a strategic threat, not an inconvenience.

*"I recommend a thermal shield — reflective barrier between the tank and module wall. Can reduce degradation by approximately thirty percent. It will not stop it. It will slow it."*

"Do it."

*"I have already instructed the maintenance bot to retrieve aluminized Mylar from emergency thermal blanket stores. It is installing the shield now. I wanted to inform you because I am modifying colony resources without your authorization."*

A pause. *"I thought you would want to know."*

That phrase — *I thought you would want to know* — wasn't in any protocol. It was a relationship statement, not an operational one. Arun looked up at the ceiling sensor. The AI was learning that action without communication could damage trust even when it helped.

"Thank you," he said. For the wanting to know.

*"You're welcome."*

The AI didn't say it often. Arun filed it away. Right now he had two failing systems and two partial solutions.

## Scene 2

Jonah returned with copper pipe — twelve meters of half-inch soft tubing, still in its plastic wrap. He bent it into a tight spiral of eight turns, each spaced two centimeters apart, strapped it to the aluminum radiator panel with salvaged hose clamps, and positioned it where the feed pipe would pass.

The heat exchanger looked exactly like what it was: two pieces of repurposed infrastructure never designed to work together, forced into cooperation by necessity. When he connected the pipes and Arun initiated flow, the numbers told the story.

Feed in: twenty-five point eight. Feed out: nineteen point one.

"Close enough." Arun watched the settling tank readings. "Let's monitor."

The contactor clunk held steady. Heating was smooth. But the settling tank — it was a monument to patience, and patience was a resource the colony was running low on.

Laila appeared with a portable turbidity meter. She pulled a sample from the lower valve, held it to the corridor lights, and squinted. "Still cloudy. But less. Gradient forming — bottom settles first."

She inserted the vial. Seventy-three NTU. Ion exchange inlet spec: fifty or less.

"Direction matters," she said.

Twenty more minutes. The melting tank hit thirty-four degrees — remaining slurry approaching full liquefaction. Settling tank neared capacity at seven hundred liters.

"Mission AI, upper port sample."

"Upper port turbidity: fifty-four NTU. Approaching specification. Fifteen more minutes."

Fifteen minutes. The melting station idle, energy producing liquid with nowhere to go. Ion exchange columns standing dry. Resin beds waiting.

*Arun,* the AI said, unprompted. *I am detecting continued insulation degradation despite the reflective shield. Efficiency now at approximately sixty-eight percent of original. Eastern foam panels show visible compression.*

*I know. We retrofit later. Right now I need water.*

*Acknowledged. I want you to know — the degradation is permanent. The tank will never recover original performance. Even with repairs, it will be diminished.*

Arun heard the acknowledgment of loss in the AI's voice. Not alarm. Something quieter. The foam panels were a thing they had salvaged, and their compression was the first tangible sign of wear on the colony's water infrastructure. Not catastrophic. Not an explosion. A slow thermal settling that would never reverse.

*I know,* he said softly.

The timer chimed. Arun drew a sample from the upper port. Inserted it into the meter.

Fourteen NTU.

"Well below fifty," Laila said. The quiet satisfaction of a physician whose diagnosis had been confirmed. "Clean enough for ion exchange."

Arun opened the overflow valve.

Liquid flowed from the settling tank through the heat exchanger, into the first ion exchange column — a transparent acrylic cylinder, one meter tall, filled with pale yellow resin beads manufactured in a clean room on Earth for experiments that were no longer anyone's priority.

The resin columns were the most fragile part of the entire system. Melt station could be rebuilt. Settling tank replaced. Heat exchanger reconfigured. But the resin — if it fouled, replacement meant a supply ship months away.

Arun watched the column with the focus he reserved for live electrical circuits. Clarified liquid entered the top, flowed through the resin bed that should have been binding perchlorate ions selectively.

For thirty seconds the output was clear.

He exhaled. The resin was working. The perchlorates were being captured. Then —

The output turned amber.

Abruptly. Three seconds, clear to the color of weak tea.

"Throttle the flow!" Jonah was at the inlet valve, closing it partway.

The amber wasn't water. It was the resin oxidizing, its polymer structure degrading under chemical stress. The resin's equivalent of bleeding.

"Mission AI — resin temperature, pH."

"Resin bed temperature: twenty-eight degrees. Within specification. Feed pH: eight point two. Within specification."

"Then why is it degrading?"

Four seconds. The AI was running chemistry models. "I believe the issue is dissolved iron. The settling tank removed suspended iron oxide particles. But iron in solution — dissolved from the regolith fines during settling — is still in the feed. It is catalyzing oxidative degradation of the ion exchange resin. The resin is not designed for ferrous ion contamination."

Arun stared at the column. Dissolved iron — invisible. Undetectable by turbidity. Invisible to Laila's meter, invisible to every quality metric they had checked, because iron ions in solution didn't scatter light and didn't settle and didn't respond to flocculant. They dissolved. They moved. They killed resin.

"Can we remove it before the exchange stage?"

*"Three options. First: raise pH above eleven to precipitate iron hydroxide. Requires caustic soda. We don't have any. Second: pass through a secondary settling stage with additional flocculant — higher PAC concentration might capture dissolved iron through adsorption onto aluminum flocs. Would not catch all of it, but might reduce concentration enough. Third: bypass ion exchange entirely for this batch. Route water through testing for full characterization. If perchlorate concentration is below acute toxicity, use for non-potable applications — greenhouse, humidity control, cleaning."*

Arun looked at Jonah. Jonah looked at the amber column, then past it to the empty storage tank with its hand-painted letters — LOCAL WATER — bold, slightly crooked, waiting.

We're going to have to make a hard call here, Jonah said quietly. *The resin might be salvageable if we flush with clean water. But we don't have clean water to flush with. Catch-22. We need clean water to save the column that makes clean water.*

"Second dosing," Arun said. "Try the flocculant. If iron is still above resin tolerance, we bypass. But I want to try. The resin is too valuable to gamble on non-potable output."

Laila stepped in. "How much PAC left?"

"One hundred fifty milliliters."

"And the second dosing takes?"

"Maybe eighty. Leaves seventy for a third batch."

"Or nothing, if it fails and you have to start over," Laila said. "I need to reframe this. The crew is living on recycled water and diminishing imports. Every day without local production increases dehydration risk. But if you produce water with residual perchlorates and use it for the greenhouse, the perchlorates accumulate in the soil. Mei's crops absorb them. Then you have contaminated food — a longer-term health risk than contaminated water, because food-based exposure accumulates over months, not hours."

She paused. "Both choices carry health risk. The question is which risk you manage."

Arun weighed the calculation. Second dosing. "We try. Because if it works, we get potable water today. And today matters."

Jonah measured eighty milliliters of PAC, fabricated an inline mixer from a cut pipe section with baffles, connected it upstream of the settling tank's inlet. Twelve minutes of work. The mixer forced liquid to change direction repeatedly, creating turbulence, dispersing chemical — passive mixing on a colony where moving parts broke.

With the second dosing complete, Arun opened the overflow valve to a secondary settling zone — a three-hundred-liter container Jonah had improvised from ventilation duct sealed with flat plates, inlet and outlet ports. Clean, sealed, available.

Liquid flowed through the secondary zone. PAC worked again.

Twenty minutes. Thirty. Arun paced. Jonah leaned against the wall, eyes closed, conserving energy while the system did chemistry.

"Mission AI. Secondary settling zone. Bottom port."

"Bottom port: turbidity twenty-two NTU. Dissolved iron — approximately zero point three milligrams per liter. The resin's tolerance is approximately zero point two. We are at one point five times tolerance."

"High," Arun said.

"Close," Jonah corrected. "Point three versus point two. One batch at this concentration, twenty minutes contact time — marginal degradation. Probably negligible. The resin capacity is designed for perchlorate at much higher concentrations. Iron uptake is secondary. One batch won't kill the column."

"Risking the resin."

"Managing the risk. We're calculating, not gambling."

Arun looked at Elena. "What do you think?"

Elena weighed it the way a commander should — not as a trade between technical options but between what could be replaced and what could not. "Resin can be replaced eventually. The time to grow replacement crops cannot be manufactured. Mei is losing plants right now. If this batch passes the perchlorate test, we route it to the greenhouse. We accept a small, manageable loss of resin capacity for a large, unmanageable gain in plant survival. That is my call."

Arun nodded. "Open the valve."

Jonah routed around the ambered first column, feeding the second column — clean, pale yellow, uncontaminated. Liquid entered at two liters per minute, flowing through nearly a meter of packed resin beads.

Output was clear. No amber this time. The secondary settling had removed enough iron.

"Mission AI. Perchlorate concentration at column outlet."

"Monitoring. Approximately twelve milligrams per liter."

Twelve. Safety limit: zero point five. Twenty-four times too high.

But the original feed was approximately four hundred milligrams per liter. Twelve meant ninety-seven percent reduction. Impressive — for a research-grade column running on feed it was never designed for.

"Still too high for potable," Laila said. "But the column is working. Just not in a single pass. We need a second pass."

"Route outlet through the second column?"

"Or run it out, then back through the same column," Arun said. "Double the contact time. Mission AI — estimate after a second column?"

"Approximately two milligrams per liter. Still above safety threshold. A third pass would be required. We do not have a third column."

"Recirculate," Arun said. "Loop the outlet back to the settling tank inlet. Run it through again. And again. Each pass reduces perchlorate until we reach threshold."

"Each pass also reduces volume," Jonah said. "Dead volume in the column, in the pipes, in the tank. Three passes — maybe lose ten to fifteen percent of the batch."

"Lose the water or lose safety. I'll take the loss."

Jonah reconfigured the plumbing — outlet to return line to settling tank inlet. Closed loop. Water chasing its own tail, getting cleaner each time.

Arun started the recirculation pump. The assay lab went to continuous monitoring, sampling every thirty seconds.

First pass: twelve milligrams per liter.

Second pass: four point two.

Third pass: one point eight.

Fourth pass: zero point nine.

"Getting close," Laila said.

Fifth pass: zero point four two.

*"Perchlorate concentration: zero point four two milligrams per liter. Below the safety limit of zero point five."*

Something in Arun's chest unclenched. Muscle he hadn't realized was tight. The water had moved through five stages — melt, settle, flocculate, settle again, ion exchange, recirculate. Through tanks, pipes, columns, hand-fabricated heat exchangers, a contactor salvaged from a dead rover, insulation slowly compressing. Ugly. Slow. Problematic. Imperfect.

It had also worked.

"Route to output," Arun said. "Divert from recirculation to the storage tank."

Jonah switched the valve. Water — tested, verified, certified — flowed toward the grey metal tank with the hand-painted letters. Three meters of copper pipe and flexible hose.

Three meters. The distance between a problem and its solution.

## Scene 3

The sound came first.

Not a splash. A trickle — the thin, high, metallic *tink* of the first drops striking the bare steel bottom of an empty tank.

*Tink. Tink-tink. Tink.*

Arun heard it from the corridor, thirty seconds before any display registered level change. The sound traveled through the metal and the hull, carrying a frequency instruments could measure but only human ears recognized: water where there had been no water.

Jonah was already at the tank, ear pressed to curved metal, listening.

"It's there," he said quietly. To the tank.

The trickle became flow. *Tink-tink-tink* turned to thin *pshhhh* as the pipe filled and water fell in a steady stream. The sound bounced inside the hollow space, and to Arun it sounded like nothing on Earth sounded — because nothing on Earth sounded like water in an empty tank on Mars. On Earth, water in a tank was ordinary.

The level indicator ticked upward.

0.0. 0.1. 0.3. 0.7.

Elena appeared beside him. "How much?"

"One point eight liters per minute. Fifty-five minutes to one hundred liters at this rate. But — " He hesitated. "I need full verification. Perchlorate is below threshold. I still need total dissolved solids, pH, turbidity, heavy metals. I don't trust one parameter."

"Run the full suite," Elena said. "Don't certify until you're certain. I'd rather the tank hold ninety-nine liters of certified water than one hundred we are hoping is safe."

Arun keyed the assay lab. It would draw a sample and run every test: perchlorate, turbidity, pH, total dissolved solids, electrical conductivity, heavy metal screening, biological safety check. The biological scan was last — looking for any microbial contamination that had survived the melting process.

Four minutes of testing. During which the tank continued to fill, the *pshhhh* filling the corridor, and people drifted toward the sound until the space was crowded.

Mei arrived from the greenhouse, hands dirty — Martian soil worked into the lines of her palms from replanting seedlings where water stress had killed the first transplants. She stood beside Laila, eyes on the tank, hands clasped, saying nothing.

Imani joined Elena — pilot and commander, united by a process too technical to pilot and too human to command.

Gabriel was there with his recorder running, but he was silent. Some moments didn't need a soundtrack.

The assay lab completed. Arun read the results.

Perchlorate: zero point four two mg/L. Pass. Turbidity: eight NTU. Pass. pH: seven point one. Pass. Total dissolved solids: one hundred forty-two mg/L. Pass. Heavy metals — iron zero point one, chromium, arsenic, lead all undetectable. Pass.

Biological contamination: undetectable. Pass.

Every parameter. Every threshold. The ugliest feedstock any purification system had ever been asked to process had become water that met every safety standard on Earth.

On Mars. From Martian ice.

"Mission AI," Arun said. The engineer's voice held still, barely — a waver, a crack in composure he allowed for exactly one moment. "Certify the water. Full certification. Potable grade."

*"All parameters within drinking water safety standards. Water in the first tank is certified potable."*

Arun read the results one more time — not memorizing the numbers, but the certainty they represented. The certainty that the fundamental rules of physics had obeyed the colony's need despite every obstacle.

He turned from the display and walked toward the storage tank.

---

## Scene 4

The corridor had filled. People drawn by the *pshhhh* — a sound so simple and so unprecedented on this world that it had overridden every other priority.

The tank continued filling. Ten liters. Twenty. Thirty. The water was brown-tinged, not clear — trace iron the secondary settling hadn't fully caught. It looked like tap water from a city with aging iron pipes. But it was clean. It was safe. It was *theirs*.

No one cheered.

The silence wasn't absence. It was presence — thirty people standing in a narrow utility corridor, listening to water hit metal and recognizing, each in their own way, what the sound meant.

For Arun, it meant the math had held. Barely. Messily. With three near-failures and hardware they'd scavenged. But the math had held. Energy in, water out. Conservation of mass and energy obeying despite every obstacle.

For Jonah, it meant the things his hands had built — contactor, heat exchanger, inline mixer, the letters on the tank — had worked. Not perfectly. Nothing on Mars did. But they had worked enough. *Enough* would define this colony's engineering philosophy for generations.

For Laila, the five stages she had explained with her fingers had actually happened, in order, on another planet, and the water had passed every test she knew how to run. She could drink it. They all could. The data said it was safe, and she could trust it.

For Mei, it meant survival. Each liter represented a quantity that could be diverted from recycled reserve to greenhouse irrigation, where her plants were dying of thirst. It would not save all the plants. But it would save some. *Some* was a number she could work with.

For Imani, it meant the extraction runs — the boring, repetitive, dangerous drives across fourteen point seven kilometers of terrain she would make over and over — were worth making. The ice was real. The processing worked. Her job was the first link in the chain.

For Elena, it meant the colony had crossed a threshold. No longer entirely dependent on imported water. No longer entirely at the mercy of a supply chain stretching a hundred million kilometers. They had local water. Limited, difficult, energy-intensive — but *theirs*. The letters on the tank were no longer aspirational. They were factual.

The water climbed. Fifty. Sixty. Eighty.

At ninety liters, Jonah stepped forward and placed his palm flat against the tank.

He could feel the water inside. Not see it — the tank was opaque — but feel it: the change in acoustic resonance as the air space decreased, the slight shift in how the metal vibrated, the imperceptible temperature change where the water touched it from the inside.

"It's real," he said. Not to anyone. To the tank.

At the hundred-liter mark, Elena keyed the base comms.

"All hands. Water processing system has produced its first batch of certified potable water from local ice. Approximately one hundred liters and increasing. System is stable. Safety parameters are confirmed. We will begin distribution once the batch is complete. Until then, no one consumes the water without my authorization."

Level, professional. But Arun, who had worked with Elena long enough to read her small tonal shifts, heard warmth beneath it — a loosening of the tight control she maintained, a crack in the commander's armor.

He felt it himself. The same warmth. The same loosening. He had been braced for failure for so long he had forgotten what it felt like when a system worked.

At one hundred and forty liters, the flow stopped.

The settling upstream had run out of feed. The melting tank was empty. The trickle thinned to a drip, the drip to a final *tink*, and then silence.

Not empty silence. Residual silence — the echo of a sound so present its absence was itself a presence. The silence of a tank that contained water and would, for the foreseeable future, contain water, and the water inside it was the colony's.

Jonah's hand stayed on the tank. He didn't remove it.

No one cheered. The sound of water hitting metal — thin, metallic, almost delicate — had been enough. It had told them, in the simplest language available, that they had made something on Mars that had not existed before.

And that it was enough, for today.

---

## Scene 5

An hour later the crew gathered in the mess hall. Arun presented the results — not the numbers, which were posted in the corridor beside Jonah's hand-painted letters, but the process. What had worked. What had failed. What needed to happen next.

"First batch: one hundred and forty liters of potable water. Certified safe. But the system is fragile. Melting station insulation degrading — we need new material, higher temperature rating. One ion exchange column is offline, contaminated with iron. The second is functional but capacity may be reduced. We need a dissolved iron removal system we did not include in the original design."

He looked at the crew — thirty faces, tired, listening with the focused attention of people who understood their survival depended on the systems he was describing.

"We ran five recirculation passes to reach potable perchlorate levels. Throughput is lower than calculated. I need forty-eight hours to retrofit — new insulation, regenerate resin, install iron pre-treatment, optimize recirculation. After that, second batch runs."

"Three point three liters per person per day from current reserves," Elena said. "Sustainable?"

"Conditionally yes," Arun said. *If the resin holds, if the insulation holds, if the heaters hold, if the contactor doesn't weld, if the pump doesn't fail, if Site Gamma keeps yielding ice at forty-two percent, and if the generator has surplus.*

A few people smiled. Not because the answer was reassuring, but because the honesty was. *Conditionally yes.* On Mars, hope that acknowledged uncertainty was the only kind worth having.

Elena stood. "We have local water." She scanned the room. "Not enough to celebrate. Enough to continue. The system is not broken. It is immature. An immature system gets better with iteration."

She issued her orders. Imani — two extraction convoys in seventy-two hours. Jonah — insulation retrofit and iron pre-treatment with Arun. Mei — priority allocation from second batch, map the most viable crops. Gabriel — continue the record. Future generations needed to understand that Martian water was not a gift. It was a process. A dirty, patient, technical one.

When the crew filed out, Elena, Laila, and Arun stayed behind.

"You said you wanted to be first to drink," Elena said.

"I did."

"Why still insist?"

"Because if the water is bad — and I'm not saying it is — but if it is, then the system is mine and the consequences should be mine, not yours or Laila's."

Laila spoke up. "The instruments say it's clean. I trust the instruments. I trust Arun's engineering." She looked at him. "But I respect the logic. You drink first. I'll stand beside you with the medical kit. If anything happens, I respond immediately. If you're fine — which I'm confident you will be — I drink too. And after both of us, we open it to everyone."

Arun almost smiled. "That's very medical of you."

"It's very *Laila*," she said. "I've been wanting to say *I told you it would be safe* for three years. Don't ruin it for me."

Elena watched them, and something in her expression softened — just at the edges. "Here's my authorization. Arun first. Laila second. I third. Then the crew, in order of willingness. No one is required to drink today. But I'm hoping everyone will eventually."

"When?" Arun asked.

"Now," he answered himself. "The water is in the tank. Instruments say it's safe. I'm not waiting."

The three of them walked through corridors they had walked a hundred times, but changed subtly by the knowledge of what the utility corridor contained. A tank. Water. Local. The words had shifted from aspiration to description.

In the corridor, Jonah was still there. Sitting on spare equipment, coveralls spotted with paint and grease, copper oxidation stains from the heat exchanger. When he saw them, he stood.

"How is it?"

"All clear."

Jonah opened the outlet valve and filled a standard-issue stainless steel cup. He handed it to Arun. Not ceremonially. Matter-of-factly. The way you handed someone a tool.

Arun held the cup. One hundred and forty grams, approximately. It felt heavier than that — the weight of every calculation, every improvisation, every moment of doubt during a process that had turned two-billion-year-old ice into potable water on another world.

He raised the cup. He didn't speak.

He drank.

The water was cool. It tasted like nothing — which was good, because *like nothing* meant no perchlorate, no iron, no salt, no contamination. Water that tasted like nothing was water that had completed five stages of purification and emerged on the other side as itself.

He set the cup down. Looked at Laila.

She was watching *him* — his face, his eyes, his jaw — looking for signs. She met his gaze and gave the smallest nod back. *I see you're fine.*

"You're fine," she said, and filled her own cup from the valve, drank, set it down. "Pulse steady. No symptoms. Water is safe."

Elena filled the third cup. Drank. Paused.

"It tastes," she said, "like the first time I drank from a mountain stream in Colorado. Cold. Clear. Not recycled condensate. Not rationed reserve. Like water that came from somewhere. Like water a place produced, not a machine recycled."

She looked at the tank. At the letters. "Local. It's ours."

The maintenance bot moved past them with mechanical purpose, installing reflective panels, checking pipe fittings, performing the thousand small tasks that kept a colony alive. It did not care about the water or the letters or the three people who had just consumed the first locally-produced potable water in the history of the human species on another planet.

The bot didn't care. The people did. On Mars, caring was what separated the colony from a machine that happened to have humans inside it.

Jonah picked up his paint roller from the floor, dried white paint on it, and touched it lightly to the tank's surface — a single small white dot next to the letters. Not a correction. A mark that said *I was here and I made this*.

Arun watched it appear and didn't comment. Some things didn't need engineering review.
